chapter_theme: A single song at Thirunallaru (திருநள்ளாறு) that turns the catalogue of a woman's body to the Goddess: the poet asks whether he will melt calling Murugan the son of Parvati, who with two measures of paddy gives charity to every house in the world; the praise names the six faces, the vel against Sura's kin and Vishnu as uncle.

808.reading: The poet lists the beauties of Parvati, breasts like green mountains, fish-like eyes, pearl teeth, coral lips, a bow-like brow, a banyan-leaf belly and a waist thin as a thread, calls her Abhirami, Mohini and the parrot, the beauty of inner experience, and the one who, settling every clan, hut and world in her house, shares out charity at all times with two measures of paddy; he asks whether he will melt calling Murugan 'Kumara' as her son. The praise names his belt and sword, twelve arms, twelve eyes and six faces, the vel that cut out the root of Sura's kin so the kalpaka heaven could live while siddhas and vidyadharas cried 'well done', Vishnu on the white serpent with Garuda, bow, conch and discus as uncle, and Murugan coming with Valli of the millet field and the elephant's daughter to Nallaru.
808.nuance: The opening uses the form the poet usually gives to courtesans, the catalogue of breasts, eyes, lips and waist, but the woman is the Goddess, and it ends in devotion, not confession. இரு நாழி நெல்லால் அறம் எப்பொதும் பகிர்வாள: the Goddess who keeps the charities with two measures of paddy, as at Kanchi. அநுபூதியின் அழகாள் may mean 'she whose beauty is inner experience'.
